steps.observation: Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
Rain needled sideways across the slate-black sea, carving faint white scratches on the water before vanishing in the foam. Ezra Cole watched through the lantern room windows as the storm rolled in, the sky shuddering occasionally with distant lightning that glowed like a lantern under a blanket.

The lamp behind him hummed faintly, its great lens glistening with reflected flashes of gray and gold. He moved with the easy, unconscious care of long practice, checking the gears, the wick, the fuel, every bolt that could loosen, every pane that could rattle. The lighthouse rose from its rock like a pale finger in the surf, three miles from shore and twenty-seven years from the last time Ezra had called any other place home.

He liked storms. They made the world honest. No pretense out in weather like this: either a ship kept clear of the teeth of the shoals, or it broke on them. Either his light burned, or it did not. The sea did not accept “almost.”

He had arrived at North Ravelin Light as a young man with a duffel bag and a secret hope that the world would forget him out here. Over the years, the world had more or less obliged. The radio brought him voices—harbor reports, weather forecasts, the occasional music program full of static—and a supply boat came on Wednesdays when the sea allowed. Once, the boat had carried a woman who stepped lightly up the iron ladder and vanished again before noon: the inspector from the Service, brisk and polite, whose questions he answered and whose signatures he watched form with a strangely fascinated distance. Other than that, there were only him, the birds, and the endless procession of ships who never saw his face, only his work.

He had once loved a girl with dark hair and a laugh like glass wind chimes. Hannah. He had planned to marry her, before her illness had swept through in a summer and left nothing behind but a ring in his top drawer and a silence in his chest that felt too large for the town. When the notice for a keeper at North Ravelin went up in the post office, he had stood looking at it until the postmaster said, “Someone ought to take it,” and Ezra found that his hand was already lifting.

Now he trimmed the wick with the same calm he had once used to comb Hannah’s hair. Routine had turned into a kind of prayer: clean the lens, oil the clockwork, log the weather, wind the mechanism, light the lamp, watch the sea. Keep the light. Keep the light. Keep the light.

By dusk, the storm was fully upon them. Waves struck the rock below with the blunt, booming sound of fists on a door. The tower trembled, old bricks murmuring in their mortar. The wind rose to a constant, wordless howl that turned the little room into a drum.

Ezra moved from window to window, checking for leaks, tasting the air for any hint of smoke or burning oil. He checked the backup generator, tested the foghorn, set his small transistor radio on the desk with the volume high. The voice from the coastal station came thin and crackling, but clear enough:

“Gale warning in effect. All small craft advised to seek shelter. North Ravelin sector visibility poor. Mariners use extreme caution.”

He allowed himself a small, humorless huff of air. “That’s what I’m for,” he said to no one.

The first glimpse of trouble came as a shadow where no shadow should be, a darker lump in the already dark sea. He saw it while sweeping the horizon with his binoculars, more out of habit than expectation. A ship’s bow, low—too low—in the water. Then a flash of white as the vessel pitched, her prow buried in a wave.

Ezra snapped the focus wheel, brought the ship closer. She was a coastal freighter, maybe a hundred and fifty feet, her deck awash, riding the storm badly. Her mast lights burned a smeared yellow, barely visible through the lash of rain.

The radio hissed as he grabbed the microphone and pressed the transmit button.

“Freighter east of North Ravelin Light, this is North Ravelin Lightstation. State your situation. Over.”

Static crackled. The speaker spat out half-words, smothered in noise.

“…engine… taking on… steering… God—”

He twisted the gain, adjusted the frequency. “Freighter east of North Ravelin, repeat your last. Over.”

A voice came through, clearer this time, frayed but young. “North Ravelin, this is the Marjorie Anne, cargo freighter out of Bellford. We’ve lost one engine and rudder control. We’re drifting. I can see your light to port. Please advise. Over.”

Ezra’s heart gave one hard thump, then settled into a sharper, more focused beat, like a drummer picking up tempo. He looked out again. The Marjorie Anne was far too close to the south, where the shoals lay like hidden teeth beneath the surface—black rock that had eaten half a dozen ships before anyone thought to build a lighthouse here.

He pulled a worn chart from the drawer, spread it on the desk, eyed the position of the ship against the sweep of his beam. If the wind held as it was, the freighter would slide sideways toward the worst of the rocks. If it shifted—

“I’ll get you clear,” he said aloud, more to himself than to them.

“Marjorie Anne,” he said into the microphone, “you are drifting toward shoals south-southwest of my position. You need to hold north of my light. Can you give me your heading and speed? Over.”

A pause, another brush of static. “This is… this is First Mate Clarke. Captain’s below with the engineer. We’re—hang on—” There was a burst of muffled shouting, the clatter of metal. “We’re trying to keep her nose into the waves, but she’s sliding. Engine’s at half, rudder’s not answering. We’ve got maybe… two knots? Feels like more. Over.”

Ezra ran a finger along the curve of the depth contours on the chart. At two knots, with this wind, they’d reach the outer edge of the shoals in under an hour. The storm wouldn’t ease before then.

“You listening, Marjorie Anne?” Ezra said. “You need to keep my light on your starboard side. If you lose sight of me there, you’re too far south. I’m going to increase the timing on my beam. Watch the flash; it’ll be your line. Hold to it as best you can. Over.”

“Roger, North Ravelin. We… we see you. Thank you. Over.”

Ezra set the microphone down, hands moving faster than his thoughts now, doing the math his mind had done a hundred times in calmer weather. The great lens behind him turned on its clockwork, throwing a thick white spear of light out into the night: three seconds on, twelve seconds off, the signature of North Ravelin Light.

He opened the panel at the base of the mechanism and flipped open the maintenance manual, though he didn’t need to. He had written little penciled notes in the margins over the years—the hum of the machine was as familiar to him as the sound of his own voice.

He wound the weight a little higher, adjusted the governor, carefully narrowing the gap on the escapement. The mechanism ticked faster, like a heart beginning to run. The beam sped up: three seconds on, nine seconds off. Enough of a change that any trained mariner would notice. Enough that, if they were watching, they could treat it as a moving marker, a living, changing thing instead of a static star.

He logged the change with quick, neat strokes in the keeper’s book, the ink spiking slightly with the tower’s shudder.

Outside, the storm raged, but his world shrank to the lamp, the chart, and the small radius of light where a freighter fought for its life.

Time thinned. It stopped being a number and became the distance between each flash of the lamp, the rhythm of the radio’s hiss, the increment of the Marjorie Anne’s crawl across the sea. Ezra reported his beacon’s change to the coast station, his short, clipped update answered by an acknowledgment and the distant promise that the lifeboat from Harbor Point was launching as soon as they could clear the breakwater.

“Won’t reach them in time,” Ezra murmured.

He returned to the window. The freighter’s lights were fainter now, half-swallowed by rain. But in each sweep of his lantern, he could see her, angling stubbornly, her bow trying to obey the wounded rudder, her stern slewing sideways like a reluctant mule. She was still north of the worst of it, but not by enough.

The tower creaked as another gust shoved at it. A droplet of water slipped down the inside of the glass, worming through an old leak. Ezra dabbed it away with his sleeve and checked the seals again by feel. No time to fix; just enough to watch, to wait, to listen.

“North Ravelin, we’ve lost your light on starboard,” the radio crackled suddenly. “I’ve got it about ten degrees to port now. We’re sliding, we can’t—”

“You’re south,” Ezra cut in. His voice carried a sternness he didn’t feel. What he felt was an echo of the sick, helpless panic that had settled into him while Hannah’s breaths had grown shorter. He had not been able to steer her away from that reef. But this—this he understood.

“Marjorie Anne, listen to me. You are heading into shoals. You cannot continue on that line. Cut your engine for thirty seconds and let the bow swing with the wind. You hear me? Cut it. Over.”

There was an outraged blast from the ship’s horn that bled through the radio, someone cursing in the background. “We’ll be broadside to the waves!” Clarke shouted. “We’ll—”

“Not for long,” Ezra replied. “You try to fight that rudder, you’ll drive her straight over the rocks. You let her swing now, the wind will push you north again. You’re three-quarters of a mile from the worst of it. You want to live to curse me, do as I say. Cut. The. Engine. Over.”

Silence reigned for a full five seconds. Ezra felt each one like a separate weight in his chest.

Then: “Engine to idle,” said Clarke, more distant now, calling it to his own crew. Another shout. Then, over the radio, more quietly: “All right, North Ravelin. On your head. Throttling down. Over.”

Ezra watched. He could not see the engine’s change from here, but he saw the ship’s attitude shift. She wallowed horribly, her nose dropping, her stern slamming into the next wave so that spray burst over her like shattered glass. For a breath, she seemed to freeze in the beam of his lantern, a fragile toy in an angry bath.

Then the wind caught her broadside and did what wind always does: it pushed. The freighter’s bow began to swing. Not much at first, reluctant, scraping some invisible resistance. Then more, a slow, grinding pivot that brought her lights back toward a line truer to his.

“There,” Ezra whispered. “There you go.”

The tower shook again. Somewhere below, a loose metal plate clanged like a distant bell. Ezra ignored it, eyes fixed on the chart, then the window, then the chart again.

“Marjorie Anne, when your compass bearing to my light reads due north-northeast, you advance to half engine again,” he said. “Not before. Call it out. Over.”

Static, breath, faint counting. Another wave smashed itself to pieces on the rock below, sending a tremor up through the floor.

“We’re at north-northeast!” Clarke’s voice came, ragged but determined. “Engine to half. Over.”

“Hold that,” Ezra said. “Keep my light just off your starboard bow. No more than five degrees. You drift south again, you cut engine again. You understand? Over.”

“Aye, North Ravelin. We’ve got you. Over.”

For the next forty minutes, that was the rhythm: light, radio, chart, sea. Ezra talked the Marjorie Anne through each tiny correction, his lighthouse’s beam the single bright line between them and ruin. Twice more he ordered them to cut power and drift, each time feeling the fury crackle through the radio at the thought of surrendering the engine to the storm.

“Trust the wind more than the rocks,” he said once, without thinking. Hannah had said something like it, once, on a hill with a wild gust tossing her hair. He had laughed then. He did not laugh now.

His voice never rose, never wavered. It was not courage so much as the inertia of someone who has done one thing, one careful, crucial thing, for so long that he could not imagine doing anything else.

At last, after an eternity measured in flashes of white and the slow creep of pencil marks on the chart, the freighter’s track nudged past the jagged cluster of warning X’s that marked the shoals. They were not safe yet; the sea could kill in deep water as well as shallow. But the teeth below them were behind.

“You’re clear of the worst of it,” Ezra said. The words slipped out with a quietness that surprised him. “Keep my light now dead abaft your beam and you’ll be in open water. Harbor Point lifeboat is on its way. You’ll hear them soon. Over.”

There was a hitch in Clarke’s breathing on the radio. “North Ravelin,” he said slowly, “we—stand by.”

The channel went silent. Ezra waited, unsettled. Had he miscalculated? Was there damage he could not see?

When the voice returned, it carried a roughness that was not interference.

“North Ravelin Light, this is Captain Harlan of the Marjorie Anne. I’m on deck now. My first mate tells me we’d be kindling on the shoals if not for you.” There was a pause, a scrape of something against the microphone, perhaps a hand rough with salt. “We can’t pay you from here. We can’t shake your hand. But you have our ship and our lives. That’s… a debt. We won’t forget your name. Over.”

Ezra stood with his hand lightly on the radio, the steady tick of the lens turning behind him, the storm pounding at the windows. For a moment, he was not a man alone on a rock in the dark; he was tied by an invisible rope to a vessel full of wet, frightened souls, their hearts beating quick and real under soaked jackets.

“Just doing my duty, Captain,” he said. It was the answer the Service manual suggested, neat and correct. But something in his chest, something that had been quiet for a long time, pushed him to add: “Get them all home. That’s payment enough. North Ravelin out.”

He set the microphone down, switched the radio back to the monitoring channel, and listened as the faint chatter of the approaching lifeboat filtered through the static. His work with the Marjorie Anne was done; now it was in other hands.

The storm did not suddenly gentled itself for having been defied. The waves still roared. The wind still clawed. But it seemed, to Ezra, marginally less vast. Not smaller, exactly—but no longer infinite. There was, out there, at least one fixed point that had held.

He walked a slow circle of the lantern room, checking once more the seals, the fuel, the slow, relentless spin of the lens. The light continued its rotation, its accelerated pattern still ticking out over the black water. He adjusted the governor back by a fraction, letting the beam return gradually to its usual rhythm. Mariners tomorrow would see three seconds on, twelve off, and note it in their logs with no sense of what had shifted for an hour in between.

Ezra logged the incident in his own careful hand. “Assisted M/V Marjorie Anne through storm conditions, possible grounding averted,” he wrote. He did not mention Clarke’s shout, the captain’s voice, the moment when the ship had hung broadside to the waves and his breath had stuck like a stone in his throat. He did not mention his own fear, or the thin thread of pride that wound through it.

When he finished, he closed the book and rested his palm on its worn leather cover. The tower groaned around him like an old animal settling into sleep.

On the desk, next to the log and the radio, sat a small photograph in a cheap frame: Hannah, twenty-two, hair blown sideways by some forgotten wind, eyes squinting against the sun as she grinned at whoever had been holding the camera. At him.

Ezra picked up the frame and looked at it for a long moment. “Still here,” he said quietly. “Still keeping the light.”

The storm fell gradually toward morning, the bruised sky lightening at the edges, the rain collapsing from needles to mist. By dawn, the sea was still heaving, but its rage had dulled into something more like a sullen sulk. The horizon reappeared as a thin gray line.

Ezra climbed down the iron stairs to the gallery outside and stepped into the wet wind. It smelled of salt and kelp and something sharp and clean that always followed a night like this. He leaned on the railing and scanned the water.

Far to the north, just at the limit of naked sight, he caught the dark shape of a ship under low clouds, moving steadily toward the safety of Harbor Point. A little white speck surged beside her—the lifeboat, guardians returning with those they’d come to fetch.

He watched until the line of land swallowed them both.

Then he turned back to the door, to the spiral stairs, to the mechanism waiting to be cleaned and the glass to be polished. The world would forget this, he knew. The sea rarely remembered the names of those who lit lamps for her. There would be no crowd, no plaque, no story passed down in warm living rooms.

But somewhere, in the wake of a freighter, men might tell the tale of a nameless voice in the dark, a light that changed its heartbeat for them. Somewhere, a captain might raise a mug in a harbor bar and say, “We owe a breath or two to a keeper on a lonely rock.”

Ezra did not need to hear that. It was enough to know that tonight, and the night after, and every night until his hands grew too stiff to turn a wrench, he would climb the steps, wind the weight, trim the wick, and send his narrow blade of brightness out across the water.

Ships would pass and never see him. They would not know his face, or the picture in the cheap frame by his logbook. But they would know, without ever forming the thought, that in this small corner of the dark there was a steadfast, patient light, maintained by an unseen keeper who had chosen to stand his watch.

He went back inside, closed the door on the waning wind, and began again.
